Runbook · reading data

Queries

Read a metric over a window, raw or aggregated, bucketed or whole-window, with the exact rules for limits, ordering, empty windows, and the point at which a query is refused for being too large.

Aggregations 10, exact — never approximate Intervals Ns/Nm/Nh/Nd, epoch-aligned Fast path hourly rollup for 5 of the 10 Row cap query.max_rows, 413 not truncation Units ns in over ZMQ, seconds in over HTTP

Asking questions of the past

Read a metric over a window — raw, aggregated over the whole window, or bucketed by the hour. Every answer is exact. A query that would be too large is refused with a reason, never quietly shortened.

Words used on this page

Window — the start and end you ask over. End is inclusive.
Bucket — one slice of the window, aligned to the epoch, not to your first sample.
Raw — the stored points, unmodified.
Rollup — the hourly summary table the fast path reads.
Watermark — the next hour the rollup will process.
max_rows — the cap on raw rows one query may materialise.
Backfill — a write whose timestamp is older than the newest stored data.
NaN — "no value". JSON has no NaN, so it arrives as null.

10
Aggregations, all exact

Three shapes of question

The same two parameters give you three different answers, and it is worth being precise about which is which.

  1. Raw — no aggregationYou get the stored points, in timestamp order. This is the only shape that returns individual measurements.
  2. Whole window — aggregation, no intervalYou get one value for the entire window, anchored at the oldest sample inside it.
  3. Bucketed — aggregation and intervalYou get one value per bucket, each anchored at its bucket start.
# 1. raw
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&limit=3&order=desc"
{"status":"ok","data":[
  {"timestamp":1790793328.2546144,"value":31.0},
  {"timestamp":1790793250.3138034,"value":31.0},
  {"timestamp":1790793028.2546144,"value":24.0}]}

# 2. whole window, every function at once
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=cpu.load&funcs=avg,sum,min,max,count,first,last,median,p95,p99"
{"status":"ok","aggregations":{"avg":59.25,"sum":12798.0,"min":20.0,
 "max":100.0,"count":216.0,"first":20.0,"last":31.0,
 "median":59.0,"p95":97.0,"p99":99.85}}

# 3. bucketed by the hour
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&aggregation=avg&interval=1h"
{"status":"ok","data":[
  {"timestamp":1790769600.0,"value":34.46666666666667},
  {"timestamp":1790773200.0,"value":59.75},
  {"timestamp":1790776800.0,"value":62.75}, …]}
Why the hour buckets start on the hour

A bucket is timestamp // interval, so it is aligned to the epoch and not to your first sample. With interval=1h the buckets are 00:00, 01:00, 02:00 — whatever time you happened to ask from.

This is what makes two overlapping queries agree. If buckets started at the first sample, asking for 09:30–10:30 and 10:15–11:15 would produce buckets on completely different boundaries, and neither could be compared with the other or with a chart someone else produced.

The ten aggregations

All ten are exact. None of them is an estimate, and none is approximate even when it is computed from the hourly summary rather than from raw rows.

NameResult over a windowEmpty windowFrom the hourly rollup?
avgArithmetic mean.NaNyes
sumTotal.0.0yes
minSmallest value.NaNyes
maxLargest value.NaNyes
countNumber of points.0.0yes
firstOldest value in the bucket.NaNno
lastNewest value in the bucket.NaNno
medianMiddle value.NaNno
p9595th percentile, linearly interpolated between the two nearest ranks.NaNno
p9999th percentile, same method.NaNno

The last column is the important one. The hourly summary stores only count, sum, min and max, so those five are answered from it and the other five must read the raw rows. That is a speed difference, not a correctness one: every answer is exact either way. min, max, avg, sum and count are also the only functions SQLite can bucket inside the database, so aggregation + interval in that set never materialises a raw row in Python.

On an empty window sum and count are 0.0 and the rest have no value. JSON cannot carry NaN, so it arrives as null:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=does.not.exist&funcs=avg,sum,count,median"
{"status":"ok","aggregations":{"avg":null,"sum":0.0,"count":0.0,"median":null}}

So a client must treat null as "no data" rather than as zero. sum = 0.0 is the mathematically honest answer for an empty set; avg = null is the honest answer for an average of nothing.

What the percentiles actually do

p95 and p99 sort the values, take rank = (n - 1) × q, and interpolate linearly between the two nearest ranks. With six values, p99 gives 50 × 0.05 + 99 × 0.95 = 96.55.

That is a choice, and it is the same one numpy.percentile makes by default. It is worth knowing before you compare a number from here with one from a tool that uses nearest-rank instead — the two will differ slightly on small samples and agree closely on large ones.

Intervals

A number and a unit, with no spaces and no separators: 30s, 5m, 1h, 1d. There is no week and no month unit.

# fine granularity, for a chart
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&aggregation=avg&interval=5m"
{"status":"ok","data":[
  {"timestamp":1790771400.0,"value":20.0},
  {"timestamp":1790771700.0,"value":27.0},
  {"timestamp":1790772000.0,"value":34.0}, …]}
Intervals that are not a whole number of hours cannot use the rollup

5m and 30m are answered by grouping inside SQLite — fast, and it never materialises a raw row in Python. But they are not served from the hourly summary, because the summary stores one row per hour and cannot answer a question about five of those minutes.

This is a speed difference only. The values are identical either way.

Limits, order, and the row cap

limit

Which end it takes from depends on order:

# the newest N points — the usual "current value" query
curl -s "…/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&limit=1&order=desc"

# the oldest N
curl -s "…/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&limit=10&order=asc"

limit must be between 1 and 100,000. Outside that you get 422 — the value is checked before the handler runs:

curl -s -w " [%{http_code}]\n" "…/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&limit=0"
{"detail":[{"type":"greater_than_equal","loc":["query","limit"],
  "msg":"Input should be greater than or equal to 1","ctx":{"ge":1}}]} # 422
limit means different things with and without an aggregation

On a raw read it bounds the SQL fetch, so a limit of 1 with order=desc reads exactly one row. On an aggregated query it bounds the number of result rows — the buckets — because the transform still needs every raw row in the window to compute them.

So limit=1 on a raw read is cheap, and on a bucketed query it means "one bucket", not "one input row".

The row cap, and why it errors instead of truncating

A query that would materialise more than query.max_rows raw rows (10,000 by default) is refused. It is not shortened, because a silently truncated answer is indistinguishable from a correct one — and you would draw conclusions from data that was never returned.

$ curl -s -w " [%{http_code}]\n" \
    "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load"
{"detail":"query would materialize more than max_rows=10000 raw rows; narrow the time
 window, use an aggregation+interval, or raise query.max_rows"} # 413

Three ways out, and only three:

FixExampleTrade
Narrow the windowadd start and end none, if you only needed part of the range
Aggregateaggregation=avg or an interval you lose individual points — which is what you wanted anyway
Raise the capquery.max_rows = 100000 more memory per query; this is the cap that bounds it

The cap is checked with a COUNT(*) before the fetch, so a refused query never pays for the rows it will not get. It applies identically to the raw path and to the hourly-rollup fast path — the cap is a property of the query, not of the route it takes.

order

asc (the default) or desc. Anything else is 422, also checked before the handler.

Where a query is answered from

Three routes, chosen automatically. You do not pick, and the answer is the same whichever one runs.

When the rollup is used

All four must hold:

  • the aggregation is one of avg, sum, min, max, count;
  • any interval is a whole number of hours;
  • the window ends at or before the rollup watermark;
  • the window spans at least two hours.

That last one is not a limitation — it is an optimisation working. For a window under two hours the raw path is genuinely faster: one partition, one index, no merge. The eligibility test exists so the fast path is used where it wins.

Why the rollup answer is exact

The summary stores count, sum, min and max per series per hour. An average over any number of hours is sum of sums / sum of counts — the same average a full scan produces, computed from sufficient statistics.

The window is split into disjoint sources: the first partial hour and the last partial hour from the raw partitions, every fully-inside hour from the rollup. Disjoint is the load-bearing word. If they overlapped, every point in the overlap would be counted twice and the average would be quietly wrong.

The current hour is always read live

An hour is summarised only after the clock passes it, and then only after waiting the client clock-skew window — so a late write can never land in an hour already summarised. The consequence is that the current, unfinished hour is never in the rollup, and is read from the raw partition instead. That is why results are never stale, and why a dashboard showing "now" is always right.

Backfills are picked up

A write whose timestamp is older than the newest data — a backfill — is the one case where the rollup needs help, because the hour it lands in may already have been summarised.

When that happens the write path rewinds the rollup watermark to the backfilled hour, inside the same transaction as the insert. The next rollup pass re-aggregates from there. Re-aggregation is idempotent, so re-rolling a range is safe and costs only the hours actually touched.

# six points spread across five already-rolled hours
# then, without any manual step:
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=spread.test&funcs=count,sum"
{"status":"ok","aggregations":{"count":6.0,"sum":249.0}}
Why this matters more than it looks

Before the rewind, a backfilled point was accepted, reported as stored, and then silently omitted from every rollup-served answer — while a raw read still showed it. That combination is the worst kind of bug: the write reported success, the data was on disk, and only the aggregate was wrong. Nothing in the API response hinted at it.

Watermarks only ever move forward, so an hour that had been passed was never revisited. Rewinding on write is what makes the rollup self-healing instead of requiring a manual partition rebuild.

The one thing still required of you: the write must be accepted in the first place. The default clock-skew guard refuses a timestamp more than 300 s from the server clock, so a genuine multi-day backfill needs ingestion.reject_client_timestamp_skew_s = 0. See Ingestion.

Results are cached briefly

Identical queries inside a 5-second window are served from a bounded cache, which is what makes a dashboard polling the same metric every second cheap rather than quadratic.

>>> st = c.admin("stats")
>>> st["query_cache_size"], st["query_cache_hits"], st["query_cache_misses"]
(2, 14, 6)

A low hit rate on a busy dashboard usually means the polling interval is longer than the cache TTL, so every poll misses. Poll faster, or ask for more per request.

The cache is bounded twice over — by entry count (512) and by total rows across all entries (200,000) — and a single result larger than that budget is never cached at all, so one huge query cannot flush everything or pin memory here.

Querying from Python

Over ZeroMQ, and remember the units: nanoseconds in the request, seconds in the reply.

>>> import time
>>> c = Client()
>>> now = time.time_ns()

# raw — nanoseconds in
>>> rows = c.query("cpu.load", start=now - 3600*10**9, end=now, limit=5, order="desc")
>>> rows
[{'timestamp': 1790793328.2546144, 'value': 31.0}, …]   # SECONDS out

# several aggregates in one pass
>>> c.aggregate("cpu.load", start=now - 7*24*3600*10**9, funcs=["avg","p95","p99"])
{'avg': 59.25, 'p95': 97.0, 'p99': 99.85}

>>> c.close()

Embedded, without a service

The same query code, in-process, with no ports. The one difference is that query returns nanoseconds, because there is no gateway converting them.

from sqtseries.engine import StorageEngine, create_sqlite_engine
from sqtseries import TimeSeriesDB

engine = create_sqlite_engine("/tmp/embedded.sqlite")
db = TimeSeriesDB(StorageEngine(engine), max_rows=10000)

# raw
rows = db.query("cpu.load", start=None, end=None, limit=10)
# [(timestamp_ns, value), ...]

# whole window
db.aggregate("cpu.load", funcs=["avg", "max"])
# {"avg": 59.25, "max": 100.0}

# bucketed
db.query("cpu.load", aggregation="avg", interval="1h")

# stream without materialising — bounded memory over a huge window
for ts_ns, value in db.query_stream("cpu.load"):
    ...

# fill gaps up to 5 minutes by linear interpolation
# (embedded API only — there is no wire parameter for it)
rows = db.query("cpu.load", fill_gaps_ns=5 * 60 * 10**9)

db.close(); engine.dispose()
Gap filling is embedded-only, on purpose

fill_gaps_ns inserts an interpolated midpoint across gaps no larger than the value you give. It is not on the wire because it changes the meaning of a result: a row you interpolated is not a row anybody measured, and a client that cannot tell the difference will average it in as though it were. Keeping it in the Python API means the caller is a programmer who can choose to use it deliberately.

The four canonical questions

These are the questions people actually ask, with the exact calls. All four outputs below are real, from the seeded example data.

1 · What was the average CPU load over the last hour?

st, en = time.time() - 3600, time.time()
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=cpu.load&start=$st&end=$en&funcs=avg"
{"status":"ok","aggregations":{"avg":62.27}}

One call. The window is one hour wide, so this uses the raw path — which is the faster route at that width.

2 · What was the peak temperature yesterday?

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=temp.celsius&funcs=max&start=…&end=…"
# ANSWER: peak_temp_yesterday = 24.49

max is rollup-eligible, so a whole-day window is answered from hourly summary rows rather than from every reading.

3 · Show me the 99th percentile response time for the past week

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=latency.web&funcs=p99&start=…&end=…"
# ANSWER: p99_latency_week = 108.00
This one reads every raw row

p99 cannot be derived from count, sum, min and max, so a week of latency data is scanned in full. That is why the row cap applies here more readily than to an average — and why, if you need a rolling p99 dashboard over months, you should either widen the cap deliberately or store hourly percentiles yourself as a separate metric.

This is the practical cost of the model, and it is worth knowing before you build a percentile dashboard rather than after.

4 · How many measurements did I record today?

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/aggregate?metric=cpu.load&funcs=count&start=…&end=…"
# ANSWER: count_today = 37

Note the trap: count is per metric. To count everything recorded today, ask each metric and add the results — there is no cross-metric count, and a series is per metric and tag set.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Empty result over ZMQ, works over HTTP seconds sent where nanoseconds were expected the request asks for 1970 — see Client Libraries
413the result would exceed query.max_rows narrow the window, aggregate, or raise the cap
504the query exceeded query.timeout_s same three options, or raise the timeout
422 on limit or order outside the accepted range or pattern limit is 1–100000; order is asc or desc
400 unsupported aggregationa typo in the function namethe ten names are in the table above
null where a number was expected an empty window, for every function except sum and count treat null as no data, not as zero
Fewer buckets than expected buckets with no data in them are omitted, not emitted empty fill them client-side from the bucket interval
An aggregate disagrees with a raw read should be impossible — please report it the equivalence is covered by the test suite

Architecture

How the hourly summary is built, and why merging disjoint sources is what makes it exact.

Raw or aggregated, and how they differ

With no aggregation you get the stored points. With aggregation alone you get one value for the whole window, anchored at the oldest sample in it. With aggregation and interval you get one value per bucket, each anchored at its bucket start.

Buckets are epoch-aligned

A bucket is timestamp // interval, not a window that starts at your first sample. With interval=1h the bucket is the top of the hour, whatever time you asked from. That is what makes two queries over overlapping windows agree.

Why some aggregates are slower

The hourly summary stores count, sum, min and max. Those five aggregations, and only those, can be answered from it. median, p95, p99, first and last must read the raw rows. The answer is identical either way — this is a speed difference only, and it is worth knowing before you build a percentile dashboard.

The rollup only covers finished hours

An hour is summarised once the clock is past it, plus the clock-skew window, so a write can never land in an hour already summarised. The current hour is therefore always read live. A query that spans fewer than two hours skips the fast path entirely: there is nothing to accelerate and the raw path is faster.

Too big is an error, not a short answer

A read that would materialise more than query.max_rows raw rows raises MAX_ROWS_EXCEEDED over ZMQ and 413 over HTTP. The check is a COUNT(*) before the fetch, so you are not charged for rows you will not get. The fix is always one of: narrow the window, add an aggregation, or raise the cap.

Results are cached for five seconds

Identical queries inside the TTL are served from a bounded cache, which is what makes a dashboard that polls the same metric every second cheap. Watch query_cache_hits and query_cache_misses on the admin socket to see it working.
